.

h

hacker, hacktivism, hacktivist

The term

hacker

is commonly used for someone who penetrates computer systems without authorization. The term originally referred to anyone with expertise in programming or hardware who tinkers with technology to understand its workings and explore new uses.

Hacktivism

consists of using computer skills as a form of protest or to try to effect change, typically in service of a cause or to expose perceived injustice. It can include defacing websites, launching denial-of-service attacks or hacking into

networks and publicly leaking information. Explain the term if writing for a general audience.

Hacktivists

are individuals with computer skills primarily driven by political or social motives rather than personal gain. They use their skills to advance a cause or expose perceived injustice. Explain the term if writing for a general audience.

While early hacktivists claimed and generally had altruistic goals, shadowy actors serving the interests of nation-states and other political forces have in more recent years conducted operations under the banner of “hacktivism” that warp its definition.

handle

A self-selected, public-facing username on a social network. May be used interchangeably with

username

.

hashtag

A term starting with a number or hash sign (#) in a social network post. It conveys the subject of the post so that it can be easily found by users interested in that subject. For example, the hashtag #UNGA is commonly used for the annual meeting of the U.N. General Assembly. A hashtag needs to be an uninterrupted string of characters, with no spaces.

The use of hashtags has evolved to also reflect a post’s tone. For example, a user may add #sarcasm or #feelingstupid to help describe the nature of a post.

When posting, take note that the use of a hashtag associated with a movement or cause could be interpreted as a sign of support. AP journalists should avoid this, unless the hashtag itself is the subject of the post. In stories, write the hashtag as it would appear on a social network:

The #Jan25 hashtag was credited with spreading support for the Egyptian uprising in its early days

.

HDMI

Acceptable on all references for

High-Definition Multimedia Interface

, a system of cables and connectors used to transmit and receive high-definition video. Commonly used to connect DVD players, digital video recorders and other video devices to television sets and computers.

HDR

Abbreviation for

high dynamic range

, a feature found in both modern displays and photography.

HDR

is acceptable on first reference, but should be explained in the story.

In video playback:

A display feature that permits brighter whites and darker blacks.

HDR

can refer to television sets, tablets and other displays with the capability. Video adapted for

internet privacy

A major issue for

Big Tech

companies and their users, particularly as governments begin cracking down on how corporations can use the personal information their users provide as part of their online activities.

Services such as

Google

and

Facebook

have long vacuumed up the personal information users share online — often

unknowingly — in order to better target digital ads or predict buying behavior. Awareness of these tactics rose substantially in 2018 when Facebook acknowledged that a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, had mined data on millions of users through a Facebook app that purported to be a psychological research tool.

Technologies such as browser cookies and mobile device IDs can follow individual users as they move across websites and use different apps. Data collected online and in the physical world via personal devices ranging from fitness trackers to smart home appliances can include users’ physical locations, recreational pursuits, home schedules, shopping and dietary habits, favorite sports teams and celebrities, vacation destinations, publications read, and television shows watched. Companies can also infer race or political views based on the types of sites visited online.

Proponents of data collection and targeted advertising say the practice makes ads more relevant to users and cheaper for advertisers. But governments, particularly in the European Union and U.S. states such as California, have since passed measures that limit how companies collect and share such data.

For instance, websites now commonly ask users for permission before saving their personal information in data cookies, a practice that once occurred behind the scenes. See

opt in, opt out

.

Companies often say they don’t sell data to third parties, a misleading statement that obscures the fact that they often make it available to advertising partners for free when users click their ads. Companies also frequently do in-house targeting on behalf of customers, allowing them to make money off user data without any need to sell it. See

digital advertising, internet advertising, online advertising

.

internet privacy laws

The United States has a patchwork of federal and state laws that cover different segments of data privacy, like health data, financial information or protections for children. But there’s no single, comprehensive federal law regulating how companies collect, store or share consumer data.

Data protections in the United States are notably different than in the European Union, which has a comprehensive data privacy law — the General Data Protection Regulation, a set of strict data privacy rules for citizens of the EU that took effect in 2018.

See

GDPR

.

internet security

As many aspects of daily life and business have moved online, so have thieves, vandals and spies. Keeping organizations, individuals and their data protected online is an increasingly challenging task that has acquired a specialized vocabulary. Some terms:

encryption

The mathematical scrambling of messages in order to shield them from unauthorized viewing or modification. Such encrypted messages can typically be read only by the sender and the intended recipient, although in the case of commercial messaging systems, the service provider can often also decrypt and access messages and data such as files, photos or video.

end-to-end encryption

A way of encrypting messages such that only the sender and recipient can read them. The messaging service does not have the ability to read or modify such messages. That also means it cannot respond to requests from law enforcement; in response, government agencies have been pushing services to create backdoors just for them, though security experts warn that any backdoor for governments could also be exploited by criminals and other

parties. Services that offer end-to-end encryption include

Signal

, Apple’s

iMessage

and Meta Platforms’

WhatsApp

,

Facebook

and

Messenger

.

No

encryption

method is foolproof, and advances in computing power and cryptographic methods can often unlock messages encrypted by older technologies. Hackers can also sometimes exploit undiscovered bugs in encryption software to illicitly read supposedly secure messages or files.

Attackers often break into seemingly secure systems by exploiting

vulnerabilities

— software or hardware flaws that can be used to bypass security protections. A

zero-day vulnerability

is such a flaw that has gone undetected by the system’s creators and security reviews; explain this term when used in stories for general audiences.

malware

A general term for software that takes harmful or surreptitious actions, usually to steal data or money, access secure systems, or disrupt organizations. Malware can spread via

phishing

, “poisoned” websites that resemble familiar destinations, apps, or by exploiting

vulnerabilities

in computer systems.

phishing

Exploits the trust of users to attack computer systems or to commit fraud by stealing personal information such as credit card numbers, Social Security numbers, user IDs and passwords. The technique typically involves doctored emails often apparently sent by friends, family or co-workers that contain attachments or links to sites that infect a user’s computer with malware.

spyware

Designed to ransack personal information, track the online activity of individuals, and sometimes to conduct surveillance via device microphones and cameras.

ransomware

Essentially holds a target computer or computer system hostage by

encrypting

its files and

demanding payment, often via bitcoin. Ransomware can target individuals, businesses and governments alike.

denial-of-service attack

Entails targeting an internet site with enormous volumes of spurious data traffic. When successful, such attacks can knock a

site

or

service

offline until their operators find a way to divert the traffic elsewhere. Sometimes abbreviated

DoS

, although this shorthand is best avoided. A

distributed denial-of-service attack

, sometimes abbreviated

DDoS

, employs a network of distributed computers to direct junk traffic at the target site.

botnet

A collection of computers infected with malware that can be centrally controlled to conduct cyberattacks. Botnets have been used to carry out

denial-of-service

attacks, spread

malware

, send

spam

and steal data. Botnets can include a variety of devices, from desktop PCs to servers to household smart devices such as internet-connected video cameras.

See

cyberattack

.

is acceptable on second reference.

intranet

A private network inside a company or organization intended for internal use.

Short for

, a numeric address given to a computer connected to the internet. Most users never see

; instead they type in domain names such as apnews.com as stand-ins for the numeric address. Background domain name servers translate from IP addresses to text and back.

can sometimes be used to identify the location of a computer, the company or organization it belongs to, and where it was registered. Avoid

the term in most stories. If necessary,

. See

domain name

Xiaomi

A Chinese company known for its value-for-money smartphones and smart devices. The company was briefly added to a U.S. Defense Department blacklist in January 2021, in the last few days of the Trump administration, which accused it of links to China’s military. It was removed from the list later that spring.

XML

Abbreviation for

Extensible Markup Language

, a structured way to encode documents containing text, data, graphics, video and more in formats that can be read by both humans and machines. Such documents can be stored, transmitted and reformatted at will.

y

Yahoo

An online services provider. Do not use the exclamation point in its formal name.

YouTube

Video-sharing service owned by Google. It has helped promote videos ranging from educational to whimsical and made celebrities out of ordinary people.

The company has faced backlash over what some consider hate speech or harassment in videos. The service made several policy changes to attempt to cut down on harassment and threats, though questionable videos still slip through. Separately, Google and YouTube agreed in 2019 to pay

$170 million to settle allegations in the U.S. that the video service failed to screen out children from using its service, thus violating a federal law that restricts data collection on children under 13.
Broadly speaking, technology encompasses all practical applications of scientific knowledge, especially in the development of tools, machinery, materials and methods of production.

These days, the term is usually shorthand for information technology such as technologies used in computing, robotics, communications and artificial intelligence, as well as the tools and processes used to manufacture devices from computer chips to smartphones to satellites. In daily usage, technology is most often used to describe internet-connected smart devices, especially smartphones; the apps they run; and the services and platforms they connect to.

Consider your audience carefully when describing technology. Younger generations have grown up with technology and require less explanation of terms and services they find familiar, while the same language may bewilder some older readers. It is safe to assume that services in widespread use — Facebook and Google, for instance — will be recognized by all demographics. Other terms, such as zero-day vulnerability, are not familiar to many and should be explained for general audiences. When in doubt, explain potentially unfamiliar terms and avoid online or technical jargon.

High technology is an outdated term for information technology. The modifier high-tech remains appropriate as a signifier of novel or unfamiliar technological developments: The restaurant’s robotic chefs prepare high-tech cuisine and serve it to diners with a minimum of fuss.

In common usage, the technology industry includes companies engaged in the development of information technology. Technology stocks are the shares of publicly traded companies in the technology industry.
Alibaba A Chinese e-commerce and online services provider.
Alphabet See Google.

Amazon Big Tech retailer of consumer products, electronics, security products, groceries, digital media and more. Amazon is also a major provider of cloud-computing services and owns the Hollywood studio MGM. Like other major tech companies, Amazon is investing heavily in artificial intelligence. See the Artificial Intelligence chapter; Big Tech.
Android The world’s most popular operating system for phones, tablets and other mobile devices. Owned by Google.
AOL An online services provider. Do not use its former name, America Online.
API Acceptable on all references for application programming interface. The term refers to software code that allows a website, app or program to interact with other websites, apps or programs.
app, platform, service, site Though these terms are often used interchangeably, they have different meanings:

An app, short for application, is software written for a mobile device or personal computer, typically for a specific task such as making airline reservations or watching Netflix. App is acceptable in all references.
A site, short for website, is an online destination typically accessed via web browsers.
A service is a function that runs on an app or at a site. Just as light bulbs tap electricity to work, apps and sites tap services to work.

A platform is a computing system composed of hardware, software, or both, on which apps and services can run, including those from third parties. The term is typically reserved for larger systems such as Facebook’s social network, Xbox video game consoles and the Windows operating system for personal computers. Apps written for one platform would typically need to be adapted to work on another.

Apple Maker of the iPhone and other personal technology devices, Mac personal computers and other products. Also a major provider of online services such as Apple TV+ and Apple Music. Apple also owns the Beats headphones company.
Like other Big Tech companies, Apple faces numerous antitrust investigations and lawsuits. See Big Tech.

app stores Lowercase references to app stores or a given company’s app store are acceptable in most instances. The game is now available in both the Apple and Google app stores. The Justice Department is investigating whether policies of the Apple app store potentially violate antitrust law. Apple and Google app stores are formally known as the Apple App Store and the Google Play Store. Microsoft’s is simply the Microsoft Store, and Amazon’s is the Amazon Appstore.
AT&T The business formerly known as American Telephone & Telegraph, today one of the largest wireless and broadband providers in the U.S.

If a human is expected to supervise or take action, the vehicle is not autonomous. In cases where a company is testing what it considers to be an autonomous vehicle on public roads with a human driver supervising, this should be called an autonomous test vehicle. Some vehicles have driver-assist systems that can perform tasks such as changing lanes, driving at low speeds, or keeping a safe distance from vehicles ahead of them, but they still need human supervision. These should be referred to as partially automated.
Avoid the term semiautonomous, because it implies that these systems can drive themselves. As of early 2024, human drivers must be ready to intervene at any time.

Nearly all automakers now sell their own version of partially automated driving systems. Some of the best known are Tesla’s Autopilot, General Motors’ Super Cruise and Nissan’s ProPilot Assist. Autopilot, ProPilot Assist and other trade names should be capitalized; the generic use of autopilot is lowercase.
avatar An image or other digital representation chosen by or assigned to users in an online service, video game or virtual reality environment.
Baidu Chinese technology company that operates a search engine and other internet services.
Avoid related jargony terms sometimes used by investors such as the now-outdated FAANG (Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Netflix, Google) unless explained and specifically relevant to markets coverage.
Bluetooth A standard for short-range wireless transmission, commonly used to establish connections between such devices as smartphones, headsets, car audio systems and smartwatches.

Blu-ray Disc A high-definition optical disc for video and other digital content that succeeded the DVD. The latest variant features 4K resolution in a format known as UltraHD Blu-ray. Such discs now face serious competition from online streaming services.
byte A unit of data storage frequently used to refer to the memory or storage capacity of phones, PCs and other digital gadgets. A byte generally is equal to 8 bits.
Abbreviate KB for kilobyte, MB for megabyte, GB for gigabyte, TB for terabyte and PB for petabyte on second and subsequent references: a 300GB hard drive.
ByteDance Chinese tech giant that owns the popular short-video app TikTok and a similar app for Chinese users, called Douyin.
CES Annual technology show held in early January in Las Vegas. Do not call it by its former name, the Consumer Electronics Show.
cloud computing The use of remote servers to store data and provide computing services to large numbers of users.

content A jargony term for the material in all forms of digital media, whether text, music, podcasts, images, video, games, augmented reality, virtual reality or others. Treat with caution and use specific descriptions instead whenever possible.
crowdsourcing The practice of asking people online to help gather information, produce ideas or conduct other tasks.

cryptocurrency A type of digital money secured via encryption technology in an unalterable — at least for now — and publicly viewable way. Cryptocurrencies make it possible to transfer value online without the need for a middleman like a bank or payment processor. As of early 2024, bitcoin, ethereum and tether were the most popular digital currencies.

miners, validators Blockchains are constructed by people known as miners or validators, who verify cryptocurrency transactions so that no one can spend the same token twice. Miners use their computing power to compete to solve a math puzzle. The first to solve the puzzle gets to add the verified transaction to the blockchain. This method is used for the bitcoin and dogecoin blockchains. Validators use a proof of stake method, where they pledge or “stake” a portion of their holdings of a particular cryptocurrency and are chosen to attest to the validity of a transaction. Ethereum switched to proof of stake in 2022. Miners and validators receive cryptocurrency as a reward.
Web3 A catchall term for the prospect of a new stage of the internet driven by the cryptocurrency-related technology blockchain.

nonfungible token, NFT Artificially scarce digital objects created by using blockchain technology to mint “unique” versions of digital artwork, sports memorabilia, famous photographs and anything else that can be digitized. NFT is acceptable on first reference, but use the full term high in the story and explain what it means.

stablecoin A type of cryptocurrency whose value is pegged to another asset, such as a fiat currency or gold, to maintain a stable price and designed to provide an alternative to the volatility of some of the popular cryptocurrencies. Tether is the most popular and largest stablecoin by market value.

cyber- In general, internet, digital or a similar term is preferred, as in internet shopping or online security. When necessary to use, follow the general rule for prefixes, which calls for no hyphen in most cases. For example: cyberattack, cyberbullying, cybersecurity. But Cyber Monday, cyber liability insurance.

darknet A part of the internet hosted within an encrypted network and accessible only through specialized anonymity-providing tools, most notably the Tor Browser. Examples of darknets include the Tor network, I2P and Freenet. Do not confuse darknets, which are generally associated with illegal or antisocial activity, and the much broader deep web.

deepfake (n., adj.) A manipulated video or other digital representation produced by sophisticated machine learning techniques that yield seemingly realistic, but fabricated, images and sounds. Deepfake video can, for instance, make it appear that people said or did things they did not actually say or do. Deepfake or deepfake video is acceptable, but must be explained on first reference. See misinformation, fact checks, fake news.

deep web A general term for portions of the internet that are not indexed by standard search engines such as Google and Bing, although they can be accessed by direct links. The deep web hosts a vast amount of legal but nonpublic activity, including private corporate websites known as intranets, secured databases, financial and medical accounts, legal files, and other data protected by paywalls or requiring secure logins. The darknet is a subset of the deep web.

device memory, device storage The memory of a computer, phone or other digital device holds data needed for current operations; it is typically wiped clean when the device shuts down. Device storage, by contrast, holds data indefinitely unless deliberately erased.

Memory and storage are both measured in bytes. Storage can take the form of a traditional magnetic hard-disk drive or a solid-state drive, which keeps data on semiconductor chips and is widely used in smartphones and other portable electronics.
search advertising Ads, usually in text, that appear alongside search results, targeted to the specific keywords typed by the user. They can also appear on third-party websites such as news sites.
display advertising A video or image ad displayed on a website or app. It can be targeted based on keywords in an article or the specific user’s personal profile.
video advertising Can include traditional television commercials shown over the internet. It can appear before or during breaks in streaming video or in a pop-up window when visiting a website.

affiliate advertising An advertising model in which a company pays a third party for bringing traffic or leads to its service or products. For example, if a third-party website posts a link to Amazon, it could receive commissions for products bought through that link.

With some services, including Google and Facebook, a business can share a list of its existing customers, based on unique identifiers such as email addresses, and have the service find other customers with similar demographics, behavior and other attributes. Facebook calls this a look-alike audience. Google calls it a similar audience.

retargeting A method of targeting an audience based on previous behavior. For example, if someone clicks on an ad or visits a shopping site but does not buy, an ad for that same product could appear later when visiting another website or app.

microtargeting The practice of targeting ads to even smaller groups of people, sometimes even individuals, by specifying a collection of user attributes to match. For example, advertisers can seek users who live in specific ZIP codes, have kids, like football, watch “Saturday Night Live” and have attended a specific school. The more specific the requirements, the narrower the audience.
pay per click A form of paid advertising in which an advertiser pays the service for every click made by visitors. Hyphenate as a modifier: pay-per-click advertising.

pay per impression A form of paid advertising in which an advertiser pays the service every time the ad is shown, regardless of whether the user clicks on the ad. Hyphenate as a modifier: pay-per-impression advertising.
click-through rate The number of clicks based on a set number of impressions.

Many services now let advertisers specify how much they are willing to pay per impression or click. The service would then display the highest bidder for a particular set of keywords or other targeting attributes. This approach is often referred to as an auction, or real-time bidding.

digital wallet, mobile wallet A phone app used to store credit cards, gift cards, loyalty cards, tickets and other transactional items. Such a wallet can include cards used for mobile payments and other digital items such as vaccination records.
The terms digital wallets and mobile wallets are acceptable, but depending on the audience, the wallet terminology may require explanation on first use. Avoid e-wallet. See mobile payment.

digitize, digitalize The term digitize generally has a narrow meaning and refers to a conversion of everyday analog information — sights, sounds, etc. — to digital form: to digitize a document. Digitalize can have a broader meaning that refers to a transformation by embracing digital technologies: to digitalize an industry.
direct message A private message sent via an online service. DM is acceptable on second reference. Can also be used as a verb: to direct-message or DM someone.

disk, disc Use disk for magnetic computer media (diskette, floppy disk, hard disk) and medical references, such as slipped disk. Use the disc spelling for optical media (a Blu-ray Disc, CD, DVD) and for disc brake.
DNS Abbreviation for the Domain Name System, an international network of directories that keep track of internet names and addresses. Spell out on first reference. See domain name.

domain name The address used to locate a website or reach an email system. In email addresses, it is the portion to the right of the @ sign. It includes a suffix that often defines the type of entity, such as .com (for commerce), .gov (for U.S. government), .fr (for France) and .bank (for financial institutions). There are also domains that use non-Latin characters such as those in Arabic and Japanese.

When writing about the suffix, use .com, .org, etc. Reserve dot-com for historical references to online businesses in the early days of the web and to the 2000 financial crash that followed the dot-com bubble. See DNS; dot-com.

dot-com An older and informal description of companies that do business mainly on the internet. Usually reserved for internet companies that thrived in the years 1995-2000, a period often known as the dot-com era. When referring to the domain name itself, use .com. See domain name.
DVD Acceptable in all references for digital video disc, similar to CD-ROMs, but able to hold more music, video or data.

DVR Acceptable in all references for digital video recorder, a feature of streaming television services that can search out and automatically record shows and movies as they are aired by cable or satellite channels. The term originally referred to stand-alone devices such as TiVo that once performed this function.

emoji (s. and pl.) A symbol, such as a cartoon face, hand gesture, animal or other object, that might be used instead of a word or as an illustration in text messages or on social media. For guidance on quoting social media posts with emoji, see quotations in the news.
emoticon A typographical cartoon or symbol generally used to indicate mood or appearance, as :-) and sometimes looked at sideways. Also known as smileys.

Facebook (company) Former name of the company Meta Platforms which owns the world’s most popular social network, Facebook. The company adopted the name Meta Platforms in October 2021 to signal its intention of building the metaverse, a proposed immersive digital environment that could in theory supplant the internet.

Facebook (social platform) The world’s most popular social network, with about 3.07 billion monthly active users as of Dec. 31, 2023. It is owned by Meta Platforms, the company formerly known as Facebook.
Family of Apps Meta Platforms’ name for its social apps and services. It includes the Facebook social network, Messenger, Instagram and WhatsApp.

fintech Short for financial technology, fintech loosely refers to products and services designed to let consumers and businesses conduct banking and other financial services digitally. It can include the technology behind mobile and online banking, money transfers among friends and tools for finding cheaper loans. Fintech can involve both consumer-facing products and back-end services and can come from both startups and established financial institutions. Fintech can be used on first reference but should be defined in the story if it isn’t clear from context.
firewall A device or software designed to stop malicious or unauthorized internet traffic from reaching a computer or local data network. Many firewalls also inspect outgoing traffic.
5G, 4G, 3G Types of mobile network technology.

5G — a shorthand term for fifth-generation wireless networks — refers to a faster alternative to the 4G mobile networks that have been in widespread U.S. service since the mid-2010s. In addition to faster speeds, 5G networks promise reduced signal lag, which can improve performance for some services.
Only newer phones updated for 5G will work with these new networks. Some providers are also using 5G for fixed mobile networks that can deliver broadband speeds to homes and businesses.
3G refers to 4G’s slower predecessor. Major 3G networks in the U.S. largely shut down in 2022, although in some other countries they are scheduled to remain operational for several years.

3G, 4G and 5G are acceptable on first reference, but should be explained in stories as cellular or mobile networks. Acceptable descriptions of 5G include faster, latest or next- generation network. Avoid the term fifth generation.
Do not confuse these terms with Wi-Fi, which describes short-range wireless networks that do not use cellular technology. See Wi-Fi.

4K The term typically refers to video with 2,160 lines of vertical resolution, producing sharper images than high-definition video. The name derives from a version that offers 4,096 lines of horizontal resolution, though the term now usually refers to a version with just 3,840 horizontal lines, also known as ultrahigh definition, or UHD. Many TVs now come with 4K capabilities even though not all movies and shows are available in 4K. 4K is considered a successor to high-definition video.
friend, follow, like Acceptable in a social media context as both nouns and verbs. Actions by which users connect to other users on social networks and engage with their content.

GDPR The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation, a set of strict data privacy rules for citizens of the 27-nation EU that took effect in 2018. GDPR has been widely described as the world’s strongest privacy law and gives people in the EU more control over their personal data. GDPR is acceptable on second reference, but use sparingly. Consider phrasing such as the rules or the privacy rules on later references.

geolocation, geotagging The act of adding geographical metadata to pieces of media, social media updates or other digital content. Also, the use of a user’s physical location to determine access to certain information. The metadata itself is an item’s geolocation or geotag. A geotagged post, photo or video would contain information about the latitude and longitude of the location where the photo was taken, or possibly the name of the city and/or country, or of a landmark or establishment where the user has chosen to check in.

GIF Acronym for Graphics Interchange Format, a compression format for images. In common usage, the term refers to images produced in this format for online use, frequently in the context of humorous social media posts.
Google Internet company that runs a dominant search engine and a major digital advertising network. Parent company is Alphabet.
Alphabet also owns several former Google-run businesses, including an investment division, a health services startup and the self-driving car company Waymo.
GPS Acceptable in all references to Global Positioning System. If a descriptive word is used following, use it in lowercase: the GPS satellite.

hacker, hacktivism, hacktivist The term hacker is commonly used for someone who penetrates computer systems without authorization. The term originally referred to anyone with expertise in programming or hardware who tinkers with technology to understand its workings and explore new uses.

Hacktivism consists of using computer skills as a form of protest or to try to effect change, typically in service of a cause or to expose perceived injustice. It can include defacing websites, launching denial-of-service attacks or hacking into networks and publicly leaking information. Explain the term if writing for a general audience.

Hacktivists are individuals with computer skills primarily driven by political or social motives rather than personal gain. They use their skills to advance a cause or expose perceived injustice. Explain the term if writing for a general audience.
handle A self-selected, public-facing username on a social network. May be used interchangeably with username.

hashtag A term starting with a number or hash sign (#) in a social network post. It conveys the subject of the post so that it can be easily found by users interested in that subject. For example, the hashtag #UNGA is commonly used for the annual meeting of the U.N. General Assembly. A hashtag needs to be an uninterrupted string of characters, with no spaces.

HDMI Acceptable on all references for High-Definition Multimedia Interface, a system of cables and connectors used to transmit and receive high-definition video. Commonly used to connect DVD players, digital video recorders and other video devices to television sets and computers.
HDR Abbreviation for high dynamic range, a feature found in both modern displays and photography. HDR is acceptable on first reference, but should be explained in the story.

In video playback: A display feature that permits brighter whites and darker blacks. HDR can refer to television sets, tablets and other displays with the capability. Video adapted for HDR uses formats such as HDR10 and Dolby Vision. HDR displays and video also typically produce a wider range of colors, although that is technically not part of HDR.

In photography: A camera feature that automatically blends multiple shots of the same subject taken at different exposures in order to prevent bright areas from being too bright and dark areas from being too dark. Some smartphones now have the feature on by default.

high definition (n.) high-definition (adj.) The term refers to video with at least 720 lines of vertical resolution. HD is acceptable on second reference. HDTV is acceptable on second reference for a high-definition television set. A U.S. DVD or analog TV broadcast has 480 lines of vertical resolution — neither is HD. Many newer TVs have even sharper resolution, with 2,160 lines of vertical resolution, also known as 4K, although not all movies and shows are available in 4K.
homepage The “front” page of a website.
hot spot Two words. Used to describe an area where computers can connect wirelessly, a troubled global locale, or an area of intense heat in general.
HTML Acceptable on all references for Hypertext Markup Language. In stories, describe as the web programming language known as HTML.

HTTP, HTTPS Acceptable on all references for Hypertext Transfer Protocol. The term has long identified the start of web addresses such as http://apnews.com, although modern browsers generally no longer display or require entry of the “http://” part. It has also been largely supplanted by HTTPS, a secure version of HTTP used to create URLs to websites whose traffic cannot be easily eavesdropped on.

IM Acceptable on second reference for instant message. Sometimes used as a verb: IM’ing, IM’d. An instant message is similar but not identical to a direct message; both offer person-to-person communication, but instant messages are usually associated with apps such as Apple’s iMessage whose primary purpose is to connect individuals or small groups. Direct messages are generally associated with broader communication platforms such as Facebook.
Instagram Photo- and video-sharing service owned by Meta Platforms.

internet A decentralized worldwide network of computers and other devices that undergirds global communications. An outgrowth of a 1960s Pentagon project, the internet blossomed as computers grew cheaper and smaller while the World Wide Web made communication simpler and more visual. The web, like email, is a service on the internet. The terms are not synonymous and should not be used interchangeably.

Internet of Things General term used to describe devices, appliances, sensors and other gadgets with internet connections. This somewhat obscure term should be avoided in stories for general readers. Instead, use internet-connected or smart, such as internet-connected thermostat or smart light bulb. See smart devices.

internet privacy A major issue for Big Tech companies and their users, particularly as governments begin cracking down on how corporations can use the personal information their users provide as part of their online activities.

internet privacy laws The United States has a patchwork of federal and state laws that cover different segments of data privacy, like health data, financial information or protections for children. But there’s no single, comprehensive federal law regulating how companies collect, store or share consumer data.

internet security As many aspects of daily life and business have moved online, so have thieves, vandals and spies. Keeping organizations, individuals and their data protected online is an increasingly challenging task that has acquired a specialized vocabulary. Some terms:

encryption The mathematical scrambling of messages in order to shield them from unauthorized viewing or modification. Such encrypted messages can typically be read only by the sender and the intended recipient, although in the case of commercial messaging systems, the service provider can often also decrypt and access messages and data such as files, photos or video.

end-to-end encryption A way of encrypting messages such that only the sender and recipient can read them. The messaging service does not have the ability to read or modify such messages. That also means it cannot respond to requests from law enforcement; in response, government agencies have been pushing services to create backdoors just for them, though security experts warn that any backdoor for governments could also be exploited by criminals and other parties. Services that offer end-to-end encryption include Signal, Apple’s iMessage and Meta Platforms’ WhatsApp, Facebook and Messenger.

Attackers often break into seemingly secure systems by exploiting vulnerabilities — software or hardware flaws that can be used to bypass security protections. A zero-day vulnerability is such a flaw that has gone undetected by the system’s creators and security reviews; explain this term when used in stories for general audiences.

malware A general term for software that takes harmful or surreptitious actions, usually to steal data or money, access secure systems, or disrupt organizations. Malware can spread via phishing, “poisoned” websites that resemble familiar destinations, apps, or by exploiting vulnerabilities in computer systems.

phishing Exploits the trust of users to attack computer systems or to commit fraud by stealing personal information such as credit card numbers, Social Security numbers, user IDs and passwords. The technique typically involves doctored emails often apparently sent by friends, family or co-workers that contain attachments or links to sites that infect a user’s computer with malware.
spyware Designed to ransack personal information, track the online activity of individuals, and sometimes to conduct surveillance via device microphones and cameras.

ransomware Essentially holds a target computer or computer system hostage by encrypting its files and demanding payment, often via bitcoin. Ransomware can target individuals, businesses and governments alike.

denial-of-service attack Entails targeting an internet site with enormous volumes of spurious data traffic. When successful, such attacks can knock a site or service offline until their operators find a way to divert the traffic elsewhere. Sometimes abbreviated DoS, although this shorthand is best avoided. A distributed denial-of-service attack, sometimes abbreviated DDoS, employs a network of distributed computers to direct junk traffic at the target site.

botnet A collection of computers infected with malware that can be centrally controlled to conduct cyberattacks. Botnets have been used to carry out denial-of-service attacks, spread malware, send spam and steal data. Botnets can include a variety of devices, from desktop PCs to servers to household smart devices such as internet-connected video cameras.
internet service provider ISP is acceptable on second reference.
intranet A private network inside a company or organization intended for internal use.

IP address Short for Internet Protocol address, a numeric address given to a computer connected to the internet. Most users never see IP addresses; instead they type in domain names such as apnews.com as stand-ins for the numeric address. Background domain name servers translate from IP addresses to text and back. IP addresses can sometimes be used to identify the location of a computer, the company or organization it belongs to, and where it was registered. Avoid the term in most stories. If necessary, IP address is acceptable on first reference with explanation, such as: Hackers targeted the site’s IP address, a numeric designation that identifies its location on the internet. See domain name.
JPEG, JPG Acceptable in all uses for the term Joint Photographic Experts Group, a common image format used on the World Wide Web.
kilohertz Equals 1,000 hertz (1,000 cycles per second). Spell out on first reference. Abbreviate kHz.

LED Short for light-emitting diode, a semiconductor device that lights up when electric current is applied. Unlike traditional light bulbs, LEDs produce light in one direction and are generally much more energy-efficient. LED is acceptable on first reference.

lidar (n., adj.) Short for light detection and ranging, lidar is a sensing method that uses pulses of laser light to determine the presence, shape and distance of objects, often in great detail. Many autonomous vehicles — excepting those made by Tesla — use lidar for guidance; the technology also has many research applications, particularly in generating precise three-dimensional renderings of Earth’s surface. It can detect objects in darkness and at times in bad weather. The term is acceptable on first reference with explanation. As an adjective: lidar sensors or lidar lasers.
Line Messaging service operated by Tokyo-based Line, which is owned largely by SoftBank and South Korean tech company Naver.
LinkedIn A social media network owned by Microsoft that’s used mainly for professional networking.
mashup A blending of two or more pieces of content, such as photos or video. For example, a video that combines audio from a song with footage from movies and overlays it with bits of text.
megahertz A measure of radio frequency or the speed of a computer processor, equal to a million hertz, or cycles per second. Spell out on first reference. Abbreviate MHz.

metadata Behind-the-scenes data that provides important information about a piece of content. Examples include information about when or where information was created, by whom and in what format. If metadata is mentioned in a story, explain what information is being revealed: Investigators determined that Johnson wrote the document by analyzing its metadata, which indicated that it had been saved on his computer.

Meta Platforms The company formerly known as Facebook, renamed in October 2021 to emphasize Mark Zuckerberg’s new goal of building the metaverse. Meta is acceptable on first reference, but use the full name somewhere in the story. Describe it as the parent company of Facebook if the context isn’t clear.

metaverse A term minted by the science fiction writer Neal Stephenson in his 1992 novel “Snow Crash,” now used to describe a proposed immersive version of the internet accessed via virtual reality headsets, augmented reality glasses, phone apps or other devices.

Microsoft A software and internet services company historically best known for its Windows operating system and Office productivity software. Microsoft also runs one of the world’s largest cloud computing operations under the name Azure and holds a major footprint in video games thanks to its Xbox family of gaming consoles.
The company has also taken a significant step into artificial intelligence by incorporating an AI chatbot based on the GPT technology developed by OpenAI into its search engine, Bing.
mips Acronym for million instructions per second. Spell out on first reference.

mobile payment Typically refers to a payment for goods or services made by tapping a phone or smartwatch near a card reader at a physical retail store or business. A form of payment previously provided to a mobile payment service, usually a credit or debit card, gets charged. Not all card readers and businesses accept mobile payments, although the number is growing.
Apple Pay and Google Pay are among the major services. Although these services are typically used for in-person payments, some also offer web and app payment options.

In a broader sense, mobile payments can also refer to sending money to friends or family through an app using a payment service such as Venmo. In some developing countries, where credit cards and bank accounts aren’t as widespread, mobile payments can refer to the use of text messaging and other means to transfer money or buy goods and services. See digital wallet, mobile wallet.

net neutrality The idea that internet service providers shouldn’t favor or discriminate against some websites or services over others. Internet service providers such as phone and cable companies typically oppose net neutrality regulations.

The company has also extended Office to include such collaborative tools as SharePoint and Teams and the cloud-storage service OneDrive. Microsoft now prefers to sell Office via an online subscription called Office 365.

opt in, opt out (v.), opt-in, opt-out (adj.) Terms used to describe how a service obtains permission for collecting and sharing data. The opt-in option requires explicit permission, while the opt-out approach typically assumes permission unless someone takes a proactive step to withdraw consent.

When writing about opt-in permission, specify how a service defines such permission whenever possible. For instance, a company with an opt-in approach may request users to accept a lengthy document that isn’t prominent or easy to understand, which users are more likely to simply accept than to read through.
Be mindful that while a company may promise to allow users to opt out of a practice, the consumer must know that the practice exists and how to opt out of it. See internet privacy.
PC Acceptable on all references for personal computer. The term typically refers to traditional desktop and laptop computers, although it sometimes includes tablets with detachable keyboards.
PDF Acceptable in all references for Portable Document Format. A file format that allows a document to be shared among multiple types of computers without losing its formatting.
Photoshop Trademark for a brand of photo-editing software. Use the generic form if the brand is uncertain.
Pinduoduo A Chinese e-commerce site that owns the Temu online shopping platform.

Pinterest A service in which users collect and share images in theme-based collections, also known as pinboards or simply boards. Images that are shared on Pinterest — or pinned — are sometimes referred to as pins. Pinterest allows people to search for and pin images as inspiration for fashion, interior design, travel and more.

record, recorded, recording Use record (or album or LP) for the vinyl discs used to play back audio. Use recording and recorded for audio also available in other formats such as CDs and digital downloads. For example: I still have several Beatles records in the attic. Streaming services account for most of the recording industry’s revenue for recorded music.

Reddit A social network that features message board-style posts organized into topic-based pages called subreddits where users share and converse. “Ask me anything” posts give users an opportunity to pose questions to public figures, topic experts and people who have had interesting experiences. AMA is acceptable on second reference.

A humanoid is a robot that physically resembles a person, though it’s still uncommon outside science fiction and research labs. Avoid calling something a robot if it is more like a remote-controlled puppet.

Artificial intelligence software can be a component of a robot, but avoid calling something a robot or robotic if it is entirely software-based, such as automated systems used in online conversation or to help make decisions. However, the term bot can be used to describe such software-based systems. A chatbot is a bot that can engage in conversations with people.
Robotics is the study and development of robots and similar machines such as drones and self-driving cars.
ROM Acronym for read-only memory, computer memory whose contents cannot be changed. ROM acceptable in all references.

Samsung Electronics Maker of appliances, consumer electronics, semiconductor chips and other products. Samsung is acceptable on first reference in stories about consumer electronics, although it is one business of the Samsung conglomerate and needs to be distinguished in broader stories about the company, Samsung Electronics.
Samsung is one of the world’s leading maker of smartphones; its most popular models carry the brand name Galaxy.
Samsung Electronics also makes television sets, refrigerators, washing machines and other consumer products. It also owns an audio and car technology business, Harman.

scraping Copying online data or content, manually or using automated scraping tools, for use or display elsewhere. Depending on what’s being scraped, this can raise intellectual property, security or privacy issues, though there are legitimate uses of the technique.

search engine optimization Any of a number of methods, both human- and machine-powered, used to improve the prominence of online content in search engines, thus increasing traffic to the content. SEO is acceptable on second reference.
selfie A self-portrait photo generally taken with a camera-equipped phone or webcam.
Signal Secure messaging service offering end-to-end encryption. That improves message security, although the service requires users to sign up with their real phone numbers. See internet security.
Sina Weibo Chinese social networking service focused on short messages, similar to X.

Skype A service, owned by Microsoft, that allows users to communicate by voice, video and instant message over the internet. Skype is used informally as a verb for using the service, particularly when communicating on video.

Slack A workplace chat service used to exchange messages and files. Often used instead of email in some settings. Do not use as a verb unless in a direct quotation, in which case it needs explanation. “She Slacked me about the upcoming meeting,” he said, referring to a message sent via the workplace chat service.
smart devices General term for a category of electronic gadgets that typically connect to the internet and offer advanced features.
In general, use two words except for smartphone and smartwatch. Many such devices are also referred to as connected, as in connected cars or connected TVs, though internet-connected is preferred.
SMS An abbreviation for Short Message Service. Text messaging is preferred.

Snapchat A service that lets users capture and share photos or video clips, often with text, drawings or other adornments. Popular among younger people, it is best known for messages that automatically disappear a few seconds after viewing. Use lowercase snap for a Snapchat posting.

social media An umbrella term for online services that people use to share posts, photos and videos with small or large groups of people, privately or publicly. Established services include Facebook, X, TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram. Others, such as China’s Sina Weibo, are popular regionally.

Messaging services such as WhatsApp and Signal are often lumped with social media but are not technically social media services. But the line has blurred in recent years, as chat services such as Apple’s iMessage, WeChat from the Chinese company Tencent and the Japan-based Line take on broader functions such as payments and group sharing.

story (on a social platform) A slideshow featuring a series of photos and/or videos that users of various social and messaging platforms — most notably Instagram, Snapchat and Facebook — can post to their accounts. The images are often adorned with text, digital scribbles or graphical elements. They typically disappear after 24 hours, though some platforms archive them for future sharing.

Tencent Chinese technology company known for the messaging service WeChat, called Weixin in China. It also owns another messaging service, QQ, along with other digital services such as video games and music and video subscriptions
text, texting, texted Acceptable in all usages as a verb for to send a text message.

TikTok Video service popular with teens and young adults. Many of the short videos are set to music and are distinguished by their lighthearted style. Parent company is Chinese tech giant ByteDance, which also has a similar app for Chinese users, called Douyin.

trending (v. or adj.) Used to indicate that a particular topic, word, phrase or piece of content is getting a lot of attention on a social network, search engine or website. Do not use without context and explanation, including describing the location of users where the topic is trending. The Oscars are trending worldwide on Instagram today.
Twitter See X.
unfollow To remove an account from the list of accounts that populate one’s feed on a social network.
unfriend To remove someone from a list of friends that one is connected to, usually on Facebook.
URL Acceptable in all references for uniform resource locator, an internet address.

USB Acceptable in all references for Universal Serial Bus, used to designate a standard interface for connecting peripherals to a computer. When the type of USB needs to be noted, use a hyphen: USB-C.

user interface The features of a device, program or website that enable control by a user. UI is acceptable on second reference. It is a key element of user experience, or UX, which is a broader term referring to how people experience a given product or service.

virtual private network A service that shields internet users by encrypting their data traffic, preventing others from observing their online activities. Organizations use VPNs for secure communications over the public internet. Individuals can also use VPN services to mask their location in order to circumvent censorship or geography-based online viewing restrictions. VPN is acceptable on second reference.

virtual reality, augmented reality Virtual reality is a computer-generated simulation of an interactive three-dimensional environment. Virtual reality experiences typically require the use of headsets, hand-held controllers and other electronic equipment that allow a person to interact with the simulation. A similar concept, augmented reality, involves the projection of interactive computer-generated images into a person’s real-world surroundings. VR and AR are acceptable on second reference.

virus, worm A computer virus is any malicious, invasive program designed to infect and disrupt computers. A worm is a type of virus that spreads on networks such as the internet, copying itself from one computer to another without human intervention.

web Short form of World Wide Web, a part of the internet that enables the distribution of image-rich content and information. The web is not the same as the internet, but is a subset of that network of networks. Other applications, such as email, exist on the internet.
When referring to websites In stories, generally use the name of the website or service rather than the web address. It’s Facebook, not Facebook.com.
web browser Software for viewing and interacting with websites on a computer or another device.

WeChat Messaging service owned by Chinese tech giant Tencent. Popular mostly in mainland China and known as Weixin in Chinese. Notable for combining functions and services that are traditionally separated elsewhere. WeChat offers basic chat features such as instant messaging and calling, and hosts group chats where users can discuss topics like sports, technology, social issues, investments and celebrities. WeChat also lets people pay for movies, food delivery, public transit and utility bills; split restaurant checks with friends; and make other payments.
widget In a technology context, a small module with a specific purpose that appears on a website, desktop or other interface and allows access to content or functions.
wiki Software that allows a group of users to add, delete, edit and share information on a website.
wireless A set of technologies for delivering data without wires. Common types include:

cellular Access comes through a phone company, such as Verizon or AT&T. Signals can travel far, offering broad coverage, but many phone plans offer a limited amount of data before charging extra and/or slowing speeds.

NFC, or Near Field Communication A wireless technology that lets two devices nearby, such as phones or sensors, communicate with each other. Its best-known use is for mobile payments, in which placing a phone near a payment reader at a store triggers the payment. NFC is acceptable in all references, but explain it.

X A social network, formerly called Twitter, on which users share text, photos, video and links with their followers in short messages. Twitter existed from 2006 until 2023. Elon Musk purchased Twitter in October 2022 for $44 billion. In July 2023, Musk renamed Twitter as X.

Use the social platform X on first reference. Reference to its former name of Twitter may or may not be necessary, depending on the story. Limit use of the verbs tweet and tweeted other than in direct quotations. Instead: posted on X, said in a post on X, etc.

Xiaomi A Chinese company known for its value-for-money smartphones and smart devices. The company was briefly added to a U.S. Defense Department blacklist in January 2021, in the last few days of the Trump administration, which accused it of links to China’s military. It was removed from the list later that spring.

XML Abbreviation for Extensible Markup Language, a structured way to encode documents containing text, data, graphics, video and more in formats that can be read by both humans and machines. Such documents can be stored, transmitted and reformatted at will.
YouTube Video-sharing service owned by Google. It has helped promote videos ranging from educational to whimsical and made celebrities out of ordinary people.

Digital

Journalism

The digital landscape is constantly changing as technology advances, user habits adapt and social media platforms innovate — or dissipate. Reading and viewing stories online is the main way many people engage with news. As such, it’s important for reporters, editors and visual journalists to understand the latest ways that readers and viewers are interacting with the news.

When writing for a digital audience, it’s important to keep copy concise, include photos/videos/interactives that add context, and keep the reader engaged. Avoid big blocks of text. And consider that many readers are looking at the content on a mobile device.

On your website, readers will find you via desktop, mobile and — if you have it — an app. Each component that goes into a story is crucial in your presentation, from headlines to images, videos and graphics. You can also put your stories in front of readers with push notifications and meet them in their inboxes with newsletters.

With social, there is no one-size-fits all approach as platforms vary vastly in offerings and presentation. A few places that you can engage with readers and build new audiences: X, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube.

All elements that feed into a story, photo or video — from the headline to the SEO title to the social graphic for Instagram — should be viewed as an act of journalism and meet the standards set by your newsroom.

Here are some guidelines to help ensure that you’re offering the best of your journalism, engaging readers, and abiding by the industry’s ethics and standards.

Visuals on social

Social visuals

are images or videos that you overlay text or other elements on to add more context.

When designing a social graphic, consider the reader experience first and foremost. On Instagram, for example, most users will be viewing the graphic on their mobile device. Think about how the photo, font and colors will appear on a screen likely much smaller than the one you are designing on.

Do not flip the photo or crop it in a way that changes its meaning.

If placing text on an image, be mindful of what you are covering up (for example, faces or key parts of the image) and avoid it when possible.

When writing headlines or creating copy for social graphics, consider how it will appear separate from the full story. You do not have the luxury of space as you would on your website. Ask yourself: Does this post stand alone, or can it be misconstrued or misunderstood?

SEO

What is SEO?

SEO

is short for

search engine optimization

. It may sound complicated, but really all it means is: What are people searching for on Google (or other search engines) and how can you ensure your content appears at the top of the search results?

Google is the primary search engine, but there are others

including Bing, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo. Search engines favor quality content that is user friendly. But remember: Journalistic integrity will always be the top priority.

How do I get my story to resonate on search?

Not all stories are going to resonate with search audiences and that’s OK. There are simple tools and ways to check whether there is search interest in a topic.

When thinking about how to optimize stories for search, put yourself in the reader’s head. What would they be searching for to learn more about a topic? Would they be typing in a specific question? What information would they want to find within the story? And what kind of headline would they choose to click on?

The best way to find out what people are searching for is to use Google Trends, or Google it yourself in an

incognito window

, which prevents your browsing history from influencing the results.

Some examples of stories that do well in search: explainers that break down complicated issues, quick hits on news that is trending, a digestible feed of live updates on breaking news, or a piece that answers a specific question. If a story falls into any of these categories, it is a good idea to invest some extra time and resources into optimizing it for search (see below).

What is a search engine result page?

A

search engine result page

is what you see from a search engine like Google when you type in a query. It is often known as a

SERP

, but avoid that acronym in copy.

What does it mean to rank on search?

Ranking on search

means your content appears high on the search results page. That can happen in a variety of ways:

In a news carousel

: If the query is particularly newsy,

search engines often create carousels toward the top of the results page to direct readers to the latest content on that topic. Appearing in this carousel often means new readers will read your content.

In an explainer box

: Sometimes there are a lot of questions around a topic and that means Google will display them on the search results page. Often it pulls from a specific story.

Below is an SEO checklist that can be used as a guide when optimizing stories for search:

Do keyword research in Google Trends to determine what people are searching for and what keywords to include in headlines/body copy.

Do simple incognito searches to see the type of content showing up and get headline ideas.

Ensure that the headline and top of story (the first 500 characters or so) have most important keywords.

Include at least two or three internal hyperlinks to other stories, as a way to show that you have authority on the topic.

Link photos and/or videos as close to publish time as possible.

SOCIAL BEST PRACTICES

All social content, no matter how small, must stand alone as an act of journalism that meets the standards set by your newsroom.

Ensure that social media posts are concise and accurate without being unnecessarily provocative or

misrepresenting a story.

For stories on complex issues, make sure your post is easy to understand for a general audience. If you’re unable to get the nuance of a story into a short post, then don’t post it.

Make sure the tone of your posts is aligned with how you want to come across. When it’s a post about a serious story, play it straight. When it’s a fun feature, have fun.

PUSH ALERTS

Push alerts are notifications sent directly to people’s mobile devices that appear at the top of their screen or on their lockscreen. They are their own medium for delivering the news. If a user clicks on the alert, they are directed to an app on the device.

A push advertises a story without the reader being able to see a preview of the story itself. It’s essentially a tap on the user’s shoulder, informing them that there is something important or fascinating that they might want to know about right away.

Writing a push alert

Like a social media post, a push alert is an act of journalism that stands on its own. As such, it must adhere to AP’s standards or those of your own organization.

Tone

The tone of a push alert should match the gravity of the story. Don’t leave the impression that you are making light of a serious topic. There are times when a word or phrase works in the context of a print story but might be open to misinterpretation in a push alert.

For breaking news, push alerts should use direct language and include context that helps readers understand why the

news is important to them.

There is more room to be creative when promoting non-breaking news.

Structure

Aim for full sentences in push alerts. If you have a lot of information that’s vital to the reader’s understanding, you can delete definite and indefinite articles (

the, a, an

). Include periods at the end of sentences in pushes.

Try to frontload the important information whenever possible.

Headline style

Push alerts should follow AP style on

headlines

, with the following exceptions:

Use periods in U.S. and U.K.

Spell out ordinal numbers (

second, ninth

, etc.)

Attribution

Attribution is important. It provides transparency so readers know they can trust what they’re reading. Whether to include attribution in the text of a push alert should be decided on a case-by-case basis. The attribution will be in the story. Ask yourself whether including the attribution in a push alert is critical to the reader’s understanding of the story.

Length

Target length for AP pushes is

140 to 150 characters

. You can go as high as 165, but it’s very likely that some of the text will be cut off on most lockscreens.
